summary: Describes Huawei's approach to bonding two GRE tunnels, one over a wired link and one over a cellular link, into a single tunnel for a subscriber. The aim is more capacity and better reliability. It is informational and documents a vendor protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Two small water pipes joined together act like one big pipe. If one breaks, the water can still flow through the other.

questions: how does gre tunnel bonding work
subtitle: Combining wired and cellular links for more capacity and reliability

tldr.problem: Service providers operate separate fixed (DSL) and mobile (LTE) networks, but customers want the combined bandwidth and reliability of both networks at the same time rather than having to choose one or the other.
tldr.mechanism: GRE Tunnel Bonding creates separate GRE tunnels over each connection (DSL and LTE), bonds them together with a control protocol, and distributes traffic across both tunnels so a single data flow can use the combined bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: A home gateway can simultaneously use DSL and LTE, offloading traffic to LTE when DSL capacity is exceeded, and maintaining service when one link fails.

today: RFC 8157 is an Informational RFC from May 2017 documenting Huawei's GRE Tunnel Bonding protocol. The protocol is deployed by service providers as a way to combine fixed and mobile access for subscribers, providing increased bandwidth and network resilience.

sections.title: Bonding Heterogeneous Network Links
sections.content:
GRE Tunnel Bonding lets a home gateway use DSL (a wired fixed-line connection) and LTE (a cellular 4G connection) at the same time, combining their bandwidth into a single virtual link.

Traditionally, a subscriber would have to pick one connection or the other, or use them separately for different applications. With GRE Tunnel Bonding, when traffic exceeds the DSL capacity, the excess automatically spills over to LTE. If one link fails, traffic continues on the other. The solution is implemented by Huawei and deployed by Deutsche Telekom AG.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscriber gets both a home broadband connection and a phone network connection, and they work together as one faster connection.

sections.title: Control and Data Planes
sections.content:
GRE Tunnel Bonding uses a two-part design: a control plane that manages the tunnels, and a data plane that carries user traffic. The home gateway (HG) sits at the customer site, and the Hybrid Access Aggregation Point (HAAP) sits in the operator's network.

The control plane uses a custom protocol that wraps control messages in GRE packets with a special protocol type (0xB7EA). Control messages set up tunnels, measure performance with timestamped hello packets, and notify each side of status changes. The data plane carries user traffic in two separate GRE tunnels, one over DSL and one over LTE, each with a unique key field and sequence numbers to maintain packet order.
sections.plainLanguage: One virtual postal worker manages the connection (control), and the actual mail trucks carry the packages (data) on both roads at once.

sections.title: How Traffic is Distributed and Recombined
sections.content:
The system classifies outgoing packets into DSL or LTE using a coloring mechanism based on bandwidth thresholds. Packets are colored green or yellow (sent over DSL) or red (sent over LTE). When the DSL tunnel reaches its committed information rate limit, excess traffic goes to LTE.

At the receiving end, packets arrive out of order because the two paths have different delays. A reordering buffer uses sequence numbers in the GRE header to reassemble packets in the original order before delivering them to the application. This in-order delivery works across both tunnels as if they were a single link.
sections.plainLanguage: Mailboxes are sorted by priority: most go on the main truck, but when it gets full, extra mail goes on the other truck. The mail carrier reassembles everything at the destination in the original order.

sections.title: Setup and Bypass Traffic
sections.content:
The HG automatically sets up both tunnels. It first acquires an IP address on each physical interface (DSL and LTE), then sends setup requests to a HAAP group. The HAAP authenticates the HG and returns its own IP address and a session ID. The two tunnels use the same session ID to indicate they belong together.

Some traffic types, such as real-time IPTV, should not be split across two paths. The HAAP sends a filter list to the HG specifying service types that bypass the bonded tunnels and use raw DSL bandwidth instead. This prevents latency-sensitive services from being fragmented.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides shake hands and agree on which types of deliveries go on which truck, and some deliveries go straight through without mixing.

sections.title: Security and Protection
sections.content:
The GRE header's Key field acts as a simple cleartext password, set by the HAAP to a random 32-bit value. Both ends validate the Key and the outer source IP address, discarding packets with invalid combinations to prevent forgery and rogue traffic injection.

The protocol is limited to single-operator scenarios, where the HG and HAAP are both operated by one service provider. For additional security, the tunnels can be wrapped in IPsec. This protection relies on the operator being trustworthy, since they can observe and potentially modify traffic between the subscriber and the HAAP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each connection uses a secret password, and mismatched or forged packages are rejected.
